activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Countries that use metres write normal vision as 6/6 instead of 20/20; both describe the same eyesight.
story:
On Monday Sadie wore her new glasses to school for the first time, and by lunch she had counted eleven things she had been missing, including the basketball hoop, the numbers on the scoreboard, and Lilou's face across the courtyard. "They're purple," Lilou said, pointing at her own glasses, which Sadie had never once noticed. "We match. Kind of." At recess a small crowd formed around Sadie near the swings, because Calum had announced that Sadie now had 20/20 vision, and everyone wanted to look at the lenses. "Actually," said a boy visiting from his cousin's school, "my cousin moved from overseas and the eye doctor there told her she has 6/6 vision. Six out of six. She says it like it's good, but that can't be good. Twenty out of twenty is perfect. Six out of six is only six."

Sadie pushed her new glasses up her nose and thought about that. If the cousin's doctor had written 6/6 on a real chart, in a real clinic, it seemed unlikely he was announcing bad eyesight. Her intuition said the numbers were measuring the same thing in different ways, like how a liter and a quart are different numbers for the same amount of juice. She needed evidence, though. "What country?" she asked. "Do they use metres there?" The boy frowned. "Yeah, kilometres and everything. My cousin says the speed signs look funny."

So Sadie proposed a test. She would stand at the fence and read the banner taped over the gym door, first with the glasses on, then off, and the group would vote on whether her vision was perfect or terrible either way. The vote to try it was unanimous, mostly because nobody wanted to go back to the four-square game while a mystery was unsolved. With her glasses on, she read every letter down to the tiny line about the spring fundraiser. Without them, the banner turned into a grey smear with a butterfly shape in the middle. "Same banner," she said, blinking. "Two different numbers could describe those eyes. Twenty twenty here, six six there. It depends on the ruler, not the eyes." She felt her ears go warm, because half the playground was listening and she was talking like Ms. Owusu during a science lesson.

The boy squinted at the fence, then at her. "So my cousin's eyes are perfect and I sent her a get-well card?" "You sent a get-well card?" said Lilou, and the crowd dissolved into laughter that was mostly with him and only slightly at him. He shrugged and said he would write a follow-up card that would preserve her dignity, something like "Congratulations on your eyes, disregard previous letter."

Ms. Owusu came out to see what the crowd was about, and when they told her, she looked at Sadie over the top of her own glasses and said that a girl who reasoned like that ought to be able to see what was sitting on her own head. Sadie reached up and found her old pair, the ones she'd been hunting for all weekend, perched on her hair like a second set of antennae. Lilou took a photo before she could take them off.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The Japanese word origami comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper.
story:
Aria spread her papers across the picnic table in her backyard, weighting the corners with pebbles because the wind kept lifting them. She was folding a paper crane for the library's origami contest, and so far she had made four cranes with crumpled wings and one that looked like it had flown into a window. Levi dropped through the gate with his own square of paper and a granola bar, and behind him came Harris, who set his phone on the table and immediately moved it again when the metal surface, already a conductor of the morning sun, grew hot under it.

"The contest rules are pretty explicit," Harris said, scrolling. "It says origami. Nothing else. So does that mean no cutting?" Levi tore the corner off his granola bar wrapper and shrugged. "My brother says origami just means paper craft. Cutting counts." Aria frowned at her fifth crane. She had a feeling that was wrong, but a feeling was not proof, and contest judges did not give points for feelings. "If the word itself tells us," she said slowly, "then we could actually know instead of arguing."

Levi leaned in, interested despite himself. Aria pulled up the library website on Harris's phone and typed the word into the search box. The entry appeared, short and plain. "Origami," she read, and then grinned. "Ori means fold, and kami means paper." Levi sat back. "So it literally means folding paper. Not cutting paper. Folding paper." Harris looked at the crumpled cranes on the table, and all three of them said it at the same time: "Start over."

They did, but Aria wanted to be sure the rule held in practice, not just on a screen. She folded one crane using only creases, and Levi made one by snipping two small cuts for the wings. They set both in the middle of the table just as dew began to condense on the cold lemonade glasses, and the wind, patient as a judge, knocked Levi's cut crane flat while Aria's folded one stayed standing. Levi laughed, but a little sadly, because he had spent twenty minutes on his. Aria slid her remaining squares of gold paper across the table to him. "You fold fast," she said. "You just got the rules wrong."

By noon there were seven cranes lined up along the table's shaded edge, one slightly lopsided but all of them made of whole paper, folded and folded and folded again. Mr. Huang, watering his tomatoes over the fence, peered at them and asked how many they were entering. "All of them," Aria said, and Levi held up his gold one, still creasing the final wing flat with his thumbnail.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Like terms can be combined before solving, so 2x + 3x becomes 5x, but 2x and 3 cannot be combined because one has a variable and one does not.
story:
The retake was at eight the next morning, and Caleb had one evening to dismantle his reputation as the kid who failed the equations quiz. He spread his notebook across the library table, where Alizee was already waiting with two pencils and a look that said she expected disaster.

"Show me what you did," she said.

He flipped to the quiz. Ms. Koné had circled one line in red: 2x + 3 = 5x. Kolton leaned over from the next chair and whistled. "You just added them? Bold move."

"It made sense at the time," Caleb said. "Two things plus three things is five things."

Alizee slid the paper back. "Try it with an actual number. Say x is ten. What's 2x + 3?"

"Twenty-three."

"And 5x?"

He stopped. "Fifty." He stared at the red circle like it was taunting him. "So they're not the same thing at all."

Ms. Koné passed their table with a cart of returns and paused long enough to tap the corner of his page. "The library closes in forty minutes," she said. "Plan accordingly."

Kolton spun his pencil. "I'm pessimistic about your chances, but go on."

Caleb wrote 2x + 3x at the top of a fresh page. This time he tested it the new way. If x was ten, that was twenty plus thirty, which was fifty, and 5x was fifty too. He tried x equal to four. Eight plus twelve was twenty, and 5x was twenty. It worked every single time, which felt almost suspicious.

"So the ones with x can combine," he said slowly, "but a plain number can't join them. It's like the x is a label. Two apples plus three apples, fine. Two apples plus three, that means nothing."

"Two apples plus three rocks," Alizee said. "You still have five objects, but you can't call them five apples."

"Right." He copied the failed quiz problem and started over: 2x + 3 = 5x became 3 = 5x minus 2x, which became 3 = 3x, and then he divided both sides by three and got x = 1. He checked it. Two plus three is five, and five times one is five. He actually laughed out loud, and a kid at the next table shushed him.

"She shushed him," Kolton whispered. "He's under siege and she shushed him."

"Do another one," Alizee said, dealing problems like cards. "Fast."

He did four more, stacking the solved pages like evidence for a trial. On the last one, 4x + 2 + x = 17, he combined the 4x and the x into 5x first, left the 2 alone, and had the answer before the clock on the wall hit the quarter hour.

Ms. Koné appeared at the desk and flicked the light switch once, the universal signal. Caleb packed his bag, then paused at the door and pointed at the last page through the window of his mind, the 5x sitting there clean and correct.

"Tomorrow," he told Alizee, "I'm getting that circle in red for a whole different reason."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Homesickness is the distress of being away from home and familiar people; it is common after a move and usually eases as a person settles in.
story:
Leah had been at Kessler Middle School for exactly four days, and she had already learned that the cafeteria had a conductor of sorts, a girl named Justina who waved people toward tables the way a train officer waved passengers aboard. On the fourth day Justina waved Leah toward a seat beside Campbell, who was drawing a map of the old Kessler building on her folder. "It used to be over on Pine Street," Campbell said. "They moved us all here two years ago." Leah looked at the map, then at her own lunch tray, and did not say that two years sounded like nothing at all.

That night she wrote a message to her best friend back in Marlow, because a phone call would make her voice shake. I keep thinking the hallway smells wrong, she typed. Like floor cleaner instead of rain. That's a weird thing to notice, right? She sent it before she could delete it. The reply came fast: not weird. My cousin says that's called homesickness. Leah stared at the word. It had a name, which meant other people had felt it too, which meant it was a thing that happened to people and not a flaw in her. She decided to test it like a science problem. If homesickness came from being away from familiar people, then the cure should be people becoming familiar, and that should take time, not willpower.

So she made a plan and stuck it inside her locker door. Rule one: say one true thing to a new person every day. Rule two: no rereading old group chats after nine o'clock, because rereading only prolonged the ache. Rule three: keep score, honestly, in the back of her notebook. Wednesday she cried in the bathroom over a photo of her old street, the crooked oak and the painted fire hydrant, and she wrote that down too. Cried, 4 minutes. It felt ridiculous, writing it, but it was data.

The next Wednesday, Mr. Eze kept her after band to ask if she would run the metronome for the flutes. "You count steady," he said. "Steady counters are rare." She counted, and Campbell mouthed a joke across the pit about a flute player who had once fallen asleep mid-note, and Leah laughed so hard she lost the count, and Mr. Eze made them all start over. That night she opened her notebook to compare. Wednesday one: four minutes of crying. Wednesday two: zero crying, one joke, one actual job. The difference was significant enough that she circled it twice.

The twist came on Friday, when Justina slid into the seat across from her and unfolded a map of Pine Street, hand-drawn, with the old school circled in marker. "I found it in my drawer," Justina said. "I looked at it every day for a month when we moved. Then I just stopped needing to." Leah understood then that the pain had a schedule, and that everyone got the same schedule, just on different days. She wrote one more message to Marlow, short this time: It gets smaller. I'm timing it. Then she closed the notebook, picked up her tray, and waved toward the empty seat beside Campbell.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach, causing the "butterflies" feeling.
story:
Amelia stood at the edge of the school parking lot, holding her phone like a ticket she was afraid to lose. On the screen was a message from Massimo: "I'm in the car with my dad. My stomach keeps flipping and my heart is pounding like I ran a mile. Can you actually be sick from a dance before the dance?" The gym doors glowed yellow behind her, and the bass from inside thumped against the parked cars.

She typed back, "You're not sick. Mr. Kaur told us last week. It's adrenaline. When you're nervous your body lets it out, it speeds up your heart, and it pulls blood away from your stomach. That's the butterflies feeling." She paused, then added, "Come anyway. If it's still happening in an hour, we'll find your dad."

Inside, Gaelle was assessing the snack table like a general planning a battle. "Brownies first, then punch," she announced. Amelia scanned the room for a way to test her own idea, because her stomach had been doing the same slow flip since seventh period. If the butterflies really came from blood being pulled away from her stomach, then getting her stomach busy with something else ought to change things. It was a concept she could actually check. She took a brownie, ate half, and waited.

By the time the DJ played the third song, her stomach had settled. She danced with Gaelle, badly, and then with a boy from science class, also badly, and laughed both times. Her heart still beat fast, but fast from jumping around, which felt completely different. She began to think the flip in her stomach might not be so inevitable after all, or at least not permanent.

Then Massimo appeared in the doorway, hair combed, shoulders up around his ears. He looked like a boy walking into a test he hadn't studied for. Amelia waved him over and pointed at the snack table. "Eat something," she said. "It works. I tested it." He gave her a skeptical look, so she told him about her stomach, and about the brownie, and how the butterflies had gone quiet.

"Adrenaline," he repeated, chewing. "Pulls blood away from the stomach. Weird that knowing it helps." He didn't finish the brownie, but he did stay. When the slow song came on, Gaelle dragged them both into a circle of friends, and Massimo's shoulders came down from his ears a little at a time, like ice melting. Near the end of the night, he leaned over during a fast song and shouted, "My heart's racing, but it's the good kind now!"

Amalie's dad was parked under the far light when the doors opened onto the cold parking lot. Massimo climbed into his own car and rolled down the window. "Text me before the next dance," he called. Amelia pulled out her phone under the streetlight and started typing.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A bar chart whose value axis starts above zero makes small differences look much bigger than they really are.
story:
Braden's kitchen felt like the inside of a sock, humid even with the fan blowing papers off the counter, and Chase had until eight o'clock to finish. The science club needed a spreadsheet showing each team's snack-stand revenue from the fall fundraiser, and as treasurer Chase had promised to email the chart to Ms. Bautista before the meeting tomorrow. He had never built one before.

"Type equals, then SUM, then open paren," Braden said, leaning over his laptop. Chase typed carefully, highlighting the column of weekly totals for Team Falcon. When he pressed Enter, the number 212 appeared at the bottom of the column, and something about seeing it add itself made him grin.

"That's the whole semester," Chase said. He did the same for Team Kestrel, which came to 218 dollars. Six dollars apart, out of more than two hundred. He clicked the chart button, chose a bar chart, and the bars appeared on the screen. Then he sat back. The Kestrel bar towered over the Falcon bar, nearly three times as tall. "That can't be right," he said.

Braden glanced at it and shrugged. "Six dollars is six dollars. Kestrel crushed you." Chase started to dismiss it and move on, but something snagged in his mind. He clicked on the chart and stared at the numbers running up the left side. They began at 200, not zero. He dragged the axis settings down so the scale started at zero, and the two bars snapped to almost exactly the same height, like two kids standing back to back.

"Look at that," Chase said quietly. "A bar chart whose value axis starts above zero makes small differences look much bigger than they really are." He turned the laptop so Braden could see the two charts side by side, the tall dramatic one and the honest one. "The first one makes it look like Kestrel doubled us. It's the same six dollars either way, but the picture lies."

Braden pulled out his phone and scrolled to the club's group chat. "Carmelo sent this chart last week. He started the axis at fifty." Chase leaned over and looked at the image, at the two bars, one looming over the other. He saved his own chart, attached it to the email, and typed a single line to Ms. Bautista: "Here are the real numbers, from zero." Then he hit send.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Stress can also show up in behaviour, such as snapping at friends, having trouble concentrating or losing interest in hobbies, and noticing these signs is the first step to managing it.
story:
Maria snapped at Bastien before breakfast, and it wasn't even about anything. He had taken the last pancake, and she had said, "Great, thanks a lot," in a voice that made Darwin look up from his oatmeal like she'd thrown it at him.

"You okay?" Darwin asked.

"I'm fine," Maria said, which was obviously untrue, since she had also lost the knot-tying contest twice this morning when she'd won it every day last week. She kept forgetting the rabbit went over the mountain, not under it. She'd skipped evening canoe practice yesterday, too, even though the regatta was Saturday and canoeing was her whole reason for choosing this camp. She had told everyone she was tired. She had not told anyone that paddling had started to feel like a test she'd already failed.

At the picnic table she made a list on her napkin. Snapping at Bastien: check. Forgetting knots: check. Skipping canoeing: check. She stared at it. Ms. Sun, the water-safety instructor, was arguing with a raccoon over a bagel two tables away, so Maria leaned toward Darwin. "If you snapped at your little cousin over nothing," she asked, "what would you think?"

"I'd think my cousin was annoying," Darwin said. Bastien kicked him under the table.

"No, I mean over nothing nothing. Like he breathed too loud."

"My cousin did that once," Bastien said slowly. "Turned out he was stressed about soccer tryouts all week and didn't know it. Stress shows up in your behavior, not just in your head. Snapping at people, can't concentrate, don't want to do the stuff you normally love." He shrugged. "My mom's a nurse. She says noticing the signs is step one."

Maria looked back at her napkin. Every single box. She felt like she'd been handed a verdict by a very small judge. "So I'm not turning terrible overnight. I'm stressed about Saturday."

"Radical discovery," said Darwin, deadpan. "The favorite canoeist is nervous about the race. Shocking."

That night, Maria tried an experiment, because a theory needed testing. She skipped the flashlight tag game, did ten slow breaths in the pattern Ms. Sun used before water drills, in for four, out for four, and got into her sleeping bag before the counselors had to yell lights-out. She did the same the next night, even when Bastien tried to lure her out by claiming he'd seen a moose, which was almost certainly Darwin in a hat.

By Friday morning she tied the knot in nine seconds flat, and at practice she caught herself grinning halfway across the lake. At breakfast she slid her own pancake onto Bastien's plate. "Truce," she said.

"I want syrup too," said Bastien.

"You're violating the truce," said Maria, and took it back.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
story:
The group chat had gone quiet in a strange way, the kind of quiet that felt louder than typing. Theo sat in the back of the science room during lunch, phone under the desk, staring at a screenshot Zara had posted in the robotics team chat. It showed a private conversation between Ellia and someone whose name was blurred out, and in it Ellia had written that Zara "always takes over everything and nobody can stand it."

"That's from a private chat," Zara said, dropping into the seat beside him. Her voice was flat, careful. "Someone sent it to me."

Theo studied the screenshot again. Ellia loved private messages; she was always typing little side comments during class, thumbs flying. She thought of them as whispers, as words that vanished. Theo had a slow, ominous feeling that he knew exactly what had happened, and it was simpler than anyone wanted to believe. A private chat was not really private, because whoever received it could screenshot it and pass it on. He tested the idea in his head: the message had reached Zara without Ellia sending it to Zara, so at least one other person had read it and forwarded it. The blur meant that person was hiding.

"Can I see who sent you this?" he asked.

Zara shook her head. "It came from a number I don't have saved. But I want to know, Theo. I want to know who's passing it around more than I even care about what she wrote."

He got that. Being talked about was bad, but being watched by someone invisible was worse, like an infection spreading through the team, quiet and unseen.

When the bell rang, Theo found Ellia at her locker. She looked pale, and her books were hugged against her chest like a shield. "Zara's not speaking to me," she said before he could open his mouth. "I said something dumb. I didn't think anyone would see it."

"Who did you send it to?"

Her eyes flicked down the hall, toward the gym doors where the team was gathering for the design workshop. "Just one person. To complain. It was stupid."

"Then it's not really Zara's problem yet," Theo said. "The screenshot came from your one person. That's where it started."

Ellia stared at him. The hallway was thinning out, sneakers squeaking somewhere far off, and Mr. Ferreira leaned out of his classroom door calling that the collaborators for the bridge project should get a move on. Ellia shut her locker with a clang.

"Come on," she said, tucking her phone into her pocket, screen down. "I'll ask Zara to show me the number."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, bowing is a common greeting, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows.
story:
The restaurant smelled of sesame and grilled fish, and Ryder stood in the doorway holding a wrapped box that was starting to feel heavier than it actually was. His classmate Emilee had invited him to dinner with her host family, a Japanese exchange student named Kenji and Kenji's grandparents, who had flown in that morning. Ryder had never met grandparents from another country before, and he wanted to make a good impression, which was exactly why his stomach was in a knot.

Kenji's grandfather saw him first. The old man stood, turned to face Ryder, and bowed, bending low from the waist and holding it for what felt like a long moment. Ryder panicked and stuck out his hand. The handshake happened anyway, awkward and parallel to nothing, and the grandfather took Ryder's fingers gently, the way you'd hold a small bird. A waiter trying to pass had to sidestep around them both, the tray of soup obstructing his view, and Ryder's ears went hot. Emilee caught his eye from the booth and mouthed, bow.

Ryder slid in beside her and put the gift on the table, which turned out to be wrong too. Kenji's grandmother frowned at it, and Kenji leaned over and whispered, "She'll take it later, when we leave. You give gifts with two hands, and she has to pretend it's too much." Before Ryder could ask what that meant, the grandmother had slid it into her bag, nodding thanks, and he decided not to test the wrapping question out loud. Instead he watched.

He watched the way Kenji served his grandfather first, the way nobody stuck chopsticks upright in the rice bowl, the way the grandfather bowed again when the tea arrived, deeper this time than before, longer too. Ryder started noticing a pattern: the shallow quick bows went to the waiter, and the deep slow ones went to the grandfather's old friend who stopped by the table. It was like the bow itself carried a measurement. Emilee saw him counting. "Kenji told me," she said under her breath. "In Japan, bowing is how you say hello, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows."

So when dinner ended and the grandparents rose to go, Ryder stood up, turned to face them, and bowed, slow and low, the way you'd mean it. The grandfather's face opened into a wide, surprised smile, and he bowed back even deeper, which made the grandmother laugh behind her hand. Kenji clapped Ryder on the shoulder. The cost was small and real at once: Ryder never got the handshake he'd practiced, and the box he'd chosen so carefully went into a bag without being opened, unwitnessed, maybe to be saved or maybe to be quietly given away. Outside, through the restaurant window, the grandfather bowed once more to the whole table, and Ryder bowed back from the sidewalk, alone.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', economist Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: it takes both to set a price.
story:
The line outside the arena already wrapped around the block when Kaitlyn and Sarah joined it, and the sky above the loading dock emitted a low rumble that could have been thunder or the sound check. Three hundred tickets, the security guard kept announcing, and Kaitlyn did the math in her head. More people than that stood behind them. "Should've bought online yesterday," Sarah said. "They were forty dollars then. The scalpers out front want ninety." Kaitlyn remembered her mother telling her to buy early, remembered shrugging and saying there'd be plenty, and the memory sat in her stomach like a stone.

A scalper worked the curb, waving tickets. "Ninety each, going fast!" Behind him another one called, "Eighty-five!" and a third, farther down, said seventy. Kaitlyn watched the prices drop as the line shrank and the sky grew more ominous. "See?" she said to Sarah. "The sellers decide the price. They're the ones calling numbers."

Sarah shook her head. "No way. People just stopped paying. The buyers decide." They argued back and forth, each pointing at the scalpers and then at the crowd, until Kaitlyn held up a hand. "It's both. It's like..." She searched for it. Ms. Do had said something once, in class, about a guy named Alfred Marshall. He wrote a book in 1890 called "Principles of Economics," and he compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors. Both blades cut. Neither one alone.

"So who's right, me or you?" Sarah demanded. "Both of us," Kaitlyn said. "That's not a contradiction, that's the scissors." Sarah still looked doubtful, but the scalper nearest them chose that moment to drop his price again, and she pulled out her wallet.

They were twenty feet from the door when the loudspeaker crackled. "Attention, everyone in line. Due to overwhelming demand, a second show has been added for tomorrow night. Tickets available now, forty dollars, no limit." The line lurched forward as half the crowd peeled off toward the box office windows. The nearest scalper stood frozen, ninety dollars' worth of paper in his hand, and Kaitlyn watched his face change as the crowd around him thinned like water running out of a sink.

He caught her eye and laughed, a short, defeated sound. "Twenty each," he said. "Take two." Kaitlyn looked at Sarah, who was already holding out a ten. Tomorrow night, then, and forty dollars left over besides. "You know," Sarah said as they counted out the bills, "I still think I was right."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Viola Spolin's 1963 book 'Improvisation for the Theater' collected theater games and is often called the bible of improv teaching.
story:
Payton sat cross-legged on the living room rug with the script she had written for drama camp, three pages of dialogue about a lost dog. She had planned to memorize it with Oskar before Monday, but when he arrived he was carrying nothing except a grin and a folded note from Mr. Ndlovu. "We're not doing scripts this week," he said, dropping onto the couch. "We're doing improv. No paper allowed."

"That's ridiculous," Payton said. "You can't make up a whole scene out of nothing. There has to be a plan." She held up her pages as evidence, as if the neat margins could refute the note itself. Oskar just shrugged and read it out loud: partner scenes, no arguing, accept every offer. Payton read it twice. The word "offer" made no sense to her, and the no-arguing rule sounded like something a counselor writes when he wants to avoid a fight rather than fix one.

Kyrie showed up ten minutes later with a canvas bag, and out of it came a battered paperback held together with a rubber band. "Mr. Ndlovu lent me this," she said, turning it so Payton could see the cover. The title was Improvisation for the Theater, and the date inside said 1963. "Viola Spolin collected all these theater games in one book. He calls it the bible of improv teaching." The spine was soft and creased, and someone had underlined the same phrase over and over: yes, and.

Payton still didn't see how two words could hold up a scene, so she decided to test it. "Fine. One scene. Oskar, you start." Oskar stood up and announced, "We're astronauts landing on a planet made of soup." Payton's first instinct was to say that was stupid, but instead she said, "Yes, and the soup is getting thicker, so we have to swim to the crater." Oskar said, "Yes, and there's a spoon the size of a bus coming toward us." Kyrie laughed so hard she slid off the couch.

They did it again, and this time Payton deliberately broke the rule to see what would happen. Oskar said, "We're pirates burying treasure," and Payton said, "No, we're at school." The scene collapsed like a dropped cake. Nobody had anywhere to go, and they stood there in the quiet living room with nothing to say. Kyrie told a short anecdote from camp about a boy who had blocked every single offer on the first day and ended up performing a scene about standing alone in an elevator, which had somehow gone on for two entire minutes. Payton laughed, but she also noticed something: the scene only moved when both people added something.

"So the 'offer' is whatever the other person hands you," Payton said slowly, "and you have to build on it instead of knocking it down." She tried the soup scene again with Kyrie, and this time Payton ended up being a mermaid who ran a lighthouse in the crater, which was not anything she would ever have planned in advance. It was messier than her script and stranger, but it moved, and it never once stopped.

By the time Oskar's mom knocked on the door, Payton had folded her three pages in half and tucked them under the lamp. Maybe she'd use them someday, or maybe she'd leave them there. She felt oddly optimistic about Monday. Kyrie gathered up the rubber-banded book, then paused and held it out. "Keep it till the weekend," she said. "Page ninety-two has the one Mr. Ndlovu says we're doing first." Payton took the soft old book and turned straight to page ninety-two.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Litmus paper only shows whether a solution is acidic or basic; it cannot tell how strong the acid or base is.
story:
Nathan's grandfather kept a cabinet above the fridge that he called "the laboratory," though it mostly held expired cough syrup and a laser level he used for hanging picture frames. Today, though, it held a small box of litmus paper, blue and red, that Grandpa had bought at a pharmacy decades ago for reasons nobody remembered. Nathan spread it on the kitchen table next to three unlabeled bottles he had found under the sink, plus a carton of orange juice from the fridge, because science required data.

Tyson leaned over his shoulder. "So you dip it and it tells you if it's an acid?"

"It tells me something," Nathan said. He tore off a strip of blue paper and touched it to a drop from the first bottle. The paper turned pink, then a solid red. Acid, apparently. He tried the orange juice next. Red again, exactly the same red, which was annoying, because the orange juice was clearly weaker stuff than whatever was in the mystery bottle, which had a smell that made Tyson back up a step and open a window.

"There's no difference at all," Tyson said, holding the two strips side by side. "That can't be right. One of them could eat through the table and the other one's basically breakfast."

Delaney, who had come over because she'd heard there would be chemicals, picked up the box and read the back. "It only shows whether it's an acid or a base," she said. "That's all it does. Not how strong." She said it flatly, like reading a bus schedule, and put the box down.

Nathan sat with that for a second. So the paper was a yes-or-no machine, and the question he actually wanted answered, which bottle would win in a fight, needed something else. He remembered Ms. Petrov, the neighbor who taught at the middle school, had once mentioned pH strips with numbers on them, a whole scale instead of a shrug. He texted her, and she walked over ten minutes later with a sleeve of strips from her classroom and an expression that suggested she found the whole situation mildly entertaining and was choosing not to say so.

"Go on," she said, handing them over, and said nothing else, which was its own kind of eloquent silence. Nathan dipped a numbered strip into the mystery bottle and watched it change, then into the orange juice, then into the third bottle, the one that had turned his red litmus paper blue, which meant base, apparently the opposite team. Tyson wrote the numbers on a napkin in handwriting like a ransom note. Delaney lined up the four strips along the table edge, red to purple to blue, a tiny color chart built out of somebody's kitchen garbage. Nathan looked at the napkin, then at the bottles, and slid the mystery bottle to the far end of the table, away from the orange juice and everyone's hands.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
Lydia dragged the old keyboard out of her grandpa's garage on a Saturday morning, coughing at the dust that rose off the cover. She had wanted to learn piano since the winter concert, when Mohammad had played a piece that made the whole gym go quiet. Afterward she had asked him how long he'd practiced, and he'd said two years, which had felt like a lifetime. Still, every Saturday since, she had come out here, plugged the keyboard into the garage outlet, and worked through the beginner book Ms. Grant had lent her from the music room.

The problem was the black keys. In her book, a song sat entirely on white keys until one measure jumped to a black one, and Lydia kept missing it. She pressed the key, listened, frowned, and pressed it again. The note sounded right sometimes and wrong other times, and she couldn't figure out why. She slid her finger along the row of black keys, noticing that they came in little clusters, two together, then three together, all the way up.

"Did you break it already?" Mohammad had biked over when he heard the keyboard through the open garage door. He set his helmet on the workbench and leaned in.

"It sounds different every time I play it," Lydia said. "Watch." She played the note, then played it again, then a third time, and on the third try it came out flat and dull.

"That's the next key down," Mohammad said. "You're sliding off. Try anchoring your thumb on the white key right below, and reach up with your finger."

She tried it, thumb planted, finger reaching, and the note rang out clean, four times in a row. "It's like the white key governs where my hand sits," she said. "If my thumb is in the right place, my finger can't land wrong."

"Exactly," Mohammad said. He ran his hand down the keyboard, glancing up at the shelf above the workbench. "You know what I did when I started? I counted the keys on my aunt's piano. She has this extravagant grand piano, gold lettering and everything, like it belongs in a monarchy's palace. I counted every single one. Eighty-eight. Fifty-two white and thirty-six black."

Lydia looked down at her keyboard, suddenly curious. She touched each white key with one finger, counting under her breath, all the way to the top. "Fifty-two," she announced. Then she counted the black ones, tapping each small key. "And thirty-six. That's eighty-eight, same as your aunt's piano." Her keyboard had fewer keys than a full piano, but the pattern of clusters matched perfectly, two black, three black, over and over, so the song book worked the same on both.

She set the book back on the stand and started the song from the top. The tricky measure came, her thumb found its white key, her finger reached up, and the black note sounded clean and true. Mohammad clapped twice against his knees. She played the measure again, just to hear it one more time.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Many of the world's hot deserts lie near 30 degrees north or south of the equator, where sinking air warms up and dries out.
story:
Connor knelt on a flat rock beside the trail and smoothed out his wrinkled worksheet, pinning the corners with two pebbles before the wind could steal it. The page showed two graphs side by side. The desert graph had temperature bars that climbed high and stayed high all year, while its rainfall bars were so short they looked like teeth on a broken comb. The rainforest graph was the opposite: temperature bars that barely changed, and rainfall bars stacked tall month after month, like a fence.

"The assignment says compare them," said Alice, dropping her pack next to his. "Ms. Bennett wants three observations by the time we reach the lookout."

"I have two already," Connor said. "The desert is hotter. The rainforest is wetter. That took me ten seconds."

"Then the third one is the hard one." Alice sat down and tapped the blank line at the bottom of the page.

Kole wandered over with Ms. Bennett's battered globe, which she let students carry on the condition that they supervise it carefully. He spun it slowly with one finger. "I keep looking at this thing while we hike. The Sahara's here. Then the Arabian Desert. Then the Thar, and the Kalahari down south." He traced a line with his fingertip. "They line up. All the big hot deserts sit in two belts, like stripes on a beach ball."

Connor frowned. He took the globe and turned it, checking Kole's stripes against the little thermometers printed on his worksheet. Something clicked. "It's not random," he said slowly. "Many of the world's hot deserts lie near thirty degrees north or south of the equator." He looked up. "That's why they're all dry. It's a pattern, like the rainfall bars on my graph. Same rule, different picture."

"So what does the air do there?" Kole asked.

"At thirty degrees, the air sinks," Connor said. "And sinking air warms up and dries out."

Alice pulled out her pencil and wrote his sentence on the third line, word for word. Then she paused. "You realize you just gave away the answer I couldn't figure out."

"You were stuck too?"

"For an hour. I was going to write that deserts are sandy." She erased a smudge. "You changed my mind about you, by the way. I thought you'd rush it and hand in two observations."

From up the slope, Ms. Bennett called that they had five minutes before the group moved on. Connor folded the worksheet along the creases and noticed the globe's rubber ring was coming loose where Kole had gripped it, the same ring that showed the territories of the endangered snow leopard stickers she'd collected over twenty years of teaching. He pressed it back with his thumb, but it wouldn't stay.

"We should tell her the globe's ripping," Alice said.

Connor stood, holding the globe against his chest where the wind couldn't catch it. "You tell her," he said. "I'll carry it to the top."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In Spanish, "¿Cuánto cuesta?" means "How much does it cost?" and is the usual way to ask the price of one item.
story:
The line at the food stalls stretched past the jewelry tables, and Isla counted four stalls selling arepas before she found the one Anne had described: yellow banner, hand-lettered sign, a woman spooning corn batter onto a griddle. Isla had spent all of Spanish class that week on food words, and she had promised herself she would order entirely in Spanish at the festival. No pointing. No English.

Phoenix was already at the front of the line, arguing with a menu. "I want the one with the cheese, but I don't know how to ask how much it is," Phoenix said. "My mom gave me ten dollars and I can't blow it all on one arepa."

That was the problem. The sign listed fillings, not prices, and the cashier kept getting pulled away to box up orders for other customers. Isla flipped through her memory of Ms. Chanthavong's flashcards, which had been tedious to make and even more tedious to drill with Phoenix at lunch. She remembered "Quisiera," which Ms. Chanthavong had made them repeat until the whole class could say it in their sleep. But price? That lesson had happened on the day Isla was at the dentist.

She reasoned it out the way she did with word problems. Spanish class had drilled question words: dónde, cuándo, quién. Somewhere in that stack there had to be a how-much word. Isla closed her eyes and heard Ms. Chanthavong's voice from Tuesday, sharp and clear: "¿Cuánto cuesta? It means how much does it cost." That had been the one card Isla kept getting wrong, the one with the pencil mark on the corner from where she'd stabbed it in frustration.

"¿Cuánto cuesta?" Isla said under her mouth, once, to get the feel of it.

When they reached the counter, Phoenix froze. Isla nudged her forward. Phoenix pointed at the arepa with white cheese and said, "Quisiera... that one," and then stopped.

Isla picked it up. She pointed at the same arepa and said, "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

The woman at the griddle looked up and answered without a pause, "Cuatro dólares." Then she added, in careful English, "You ask right. That is the way to ask for one."

"Four dollars," Isla translated for Phoenix. Phoenix counted out a five, took the change, and held up the wrapped arepa like a trophy.

"Say the whole thing," Phoenix said. "Order for me too. I'll owe you one."

Isla turned back to the counter. The steam from the griddle smelled of toasted corn and melted cheese. "Quisiera una arepa con queso," she said, and then, because it was the part she was proudest of, "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

"Cuatro," the woman said again, and smiled. Isla dug out her crumpled bills and laid them on the counter one by one.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Researchers usually define bullying as hurtful behavior that is repeated and involves an imbalance of power, unlike a one-time argument between equals.
story:
The third time that week, someone knocked Darius's sketchbook off his desk on the way past, and the whole back row laughed. Mathis counted in his head. Monday it had been "accidental." Tuesday, "a joke." Wednesday, nobody even bothered with a word. He looked at the kid who did it, Trent-sized and confident, then at Darius, who picked up the book, checked a bent corner, and said nothing.

At lunch Mathis sat across from Margo, who was eating fries one at a time like she was rationing them. "Remember last month when you and I yelled at each other about the group project?" he said. "That was bad. But we're equals. We both got mad, we both apologized, it was over." Margo raised an eyebrow. "Is this a peace treaty or a thought?" "A thought," Mathis said. "What keeps happening to Darius isn't that. It's happened over and over, and Trent's got the whole back row behind him. That's not a fight between equals. That's an imbalance of power." Margo dunked a fry. "So it's not just joking around." "Researchers usually define bullying that way," Mathis said. "Hurtful behavior, repeated, with a power imbalance. One-time arguments between equals don't count."

The tricky part was what to do about it. Mathis had already tried the obvious version in seventh grade, when he'd stood up in class and called a kid a word he wouldn't repeat at home. That had made everything worse, like a virus that spread through the whole grade by Friday, and his help had lasted exactly as long as the teacher's attention, which was to say temporary.

So on Thursday, when Trent's hand drifted toward Darius's sketchbook, Mathis slid his own binder across the aisle first, so the desk was crowded. "Hey, Darius," he said, loud enough for the back row, "let me see that dragon from yesterday." Darius blinked, then turned the pages. The hand retreated, since knocking a book two kids were looking at was harder to interpret as an accident.

Mr. Clarke looked up from his attendance sheet. "Everything all right over there?" "Fine," Mathis said. "Just admiring the dragon." It was, in fact, a very good dragon.

Between classes, Margo caught up with him at the water fountain. "You didn't beat anybody up. Impressive restraint." "You'd be amazed," Mathis said. Down the hall, Darius was walking with his sketchbook held flat and safe against his chest, and he glanced back at them and lifted it slightly, like a toast.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A person who has memorized the entire Quran, all 114 chapters, is called a hafiz, and keeping it perfectly remembered takes constant practice.
story:
Jaxon stood at the back of the community hall with his index card of Arabic script trembling in his hand, wishing he could somehow dismantle the whole ceremony and hide the pieces. In two weeks he would stand at the front and recite Surah Al-Mulk from memory, and so far he could get through about four verses before everything fell apart. Across the hall, his cousin Ibrahim was helping Mr. Suzuki arrange the folding chairs for Thursday practice, and something about the way Ibrahim moved made Jaxon stop worrying about himself for a moment. Ibrahim never carried a card. Ibrahim never carried anything at all.

Last summer, Jaxon remembered, he had walked into the kitchen and found Ibrahim making sandwiches while reciting out loud, his voice rising and falling like he was singing to the bread. When Jaxon asked what he was doing, Ibrahim had only laughed and said, "Practice." At the time Jaxon had thought that was a strange thing to do with your hands full of mustard, but now, watching his cousin space the chairs without pausing, a question began to form in his mind.

He crossed the hall. "Ibrahim, do you still have to practice? You already know everything."

"I'm a hafiz," Ibrahim said, and then he began reciting the very surah Jaxon was struggling with, all thirty verses, without a single hesitation, without even looking up from the chair he was stacking. When he finished, he smiled. "All 114 chapters, in here. But keeping it perfect takes constant practice. Every day. It never stops."

Jaxon stared at him. Here was a person who had memorized the entire Quran, and he still practiced daily like a beginner? That seemed unfair, like reaching the top of a mountain and being told you have to keep climbing. But then a pattern suggested itself, one that felt almost too plausible: maybe memory was not a door you walked through once. Maybe it was a garden that needed watering, or the verses would wilt. He had assumed that once he learned his surah, the work would be over. Now he wondered if that whole idea was wrong.

"Can I try something?" Jaxon said. He put the index card in his pocket, closed his eyes, and recited the first four verses, the ones he knew. When he opened his eyes, Ibrahim was nodding, and near the stage Laurel and Brynn had stopped their conversation to listen. "You dropped a vowel in verse three," Brynn called out. "We've been listening to you practice all month. You're getting closer."

So that was the solution, Jaxon realized. He would practice every single day, even after the ceremony, and he would ask Laurel and Brynn to catch his mistakes. He walked to the front of the hall, took a breath, and began again from verse one, his voice steadier than it had been all month, while Ibrahim stacked the last chair and listened.

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: Japanese has no separate future tense: one verb form, called the non-past, covers both present and future, and a time word like "rainen" (next year) shows when.
story:
Ava stared at the blank worksheet in front of her and wrote three words in careful Japanese script, then crossed them out. Ms. Asante had asked everyone to write a paragraph about plans for next year, and Trace was already on his fourth sentence, his pencil moving like it knew where it was going. Ava's pencil did not.

"Stuck again?" Jia whispered from the next desk.

"Every verb I look up looks wrong for future stuff." Ava turned her notebook so Jia could see. "I want to say I will join the art club next year. But the verb just sits there like it means now. Like I'm joining it at this exact second, at this desk."

Trace leaned over. "Mine does the same thing. Watch." He read his sentence aloud, then translated it. "I go to Kyoto. Present tense, right? But I meant next year."

"That can't be right," Jia said. "There has to be a future form somewhere in the book."

Ava flipped to the verb chart at the back. She checked every form listed, then checked again, adjusting her grip on the page as if holding it differently might reveal a row she had missed. There was no future row. Present and future shared one column. Ms. Asante walked past, and Ava raised her hand before she could think better of it.

"Ms. Asante, if I say ikimasu, how does anyone know if I mean now or later?"

Ms. Asante smiled but didn't stop walking. "Try saying your sentence twice to your group. Once with a time word, once without. Listen for what changes."

Ava felt her intuition poke at her, the same feeling she'd had last month when she'd guessed a spelling rule and been wrong in front of everyone. She hesitated, remembering that. Then she tried it anyway, reading Trace's sentence without any time word, then with "rainen" at the front.

"It still sounds present without the time word," Jia said slowly. "But with rainen in there, it means next year. Same verb."

"So the verb doesn't change at all?" Trace wrote rainen beside his sentence. "One form does both?"

Jia nodded. "It's called the non-past. I read that last night and thought it was a typo."

Ava tested it with her own sentence, slotting rainen into the front. The verb stayed exactly as it was, and somehow the whole thing now pointed forward, toward an art club and a year that hadn't happened yet. She checked her other sentences and found the pattern was consistent: wherever the time word went, the verb never moved. That was the whole trick, and it had been sitting in the chart the entire time.

She began writing her paragraph, sentence by sentence, her pencil steady now. Next to her, Trace drew a small box around rainen on his paper and underlined it twice.

"This," he said, "is going on the wall of my brain."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games, an effect called home advantage.
story:
The whole crowd at Mr. Grewal's house groaned at once when the tying shot bounced off the rim, and Kate heard her dad's voice crack above the rest. She was squeezed onto the couch between Kohen and Darius, sharing a bowl of popcorn that was mostly crumbs now, watching the final seconds of the playoff game. When the buzzer sounded, the home team had won by three.

"See, they're the best team in the league," Darius said, pumping his fist. "Nobody can beat them."

Kohen shook his head. "They only won because they played at home. Put them in the other guys' arena and they lose. That's all it is."

Kate frowned at the screen, where the players were hugging and the crowd was spilling toward the exits. She thought about the season they had just watched. The team had looked unstoppable in this building, but she remembered a road trip in February when they had dropped three games in a row. "There might be something real in that," she said. "But you're saying it like it's just an excuse, and I don't think you actually know."

Mr. Grewal leaned over from his armchair. "You two could settle it, you know. It wouldn't take long."

Kate borrowed his tablet and pulled up the team's season results. She grabbed a napkin from the snack table and started to document every game, marking an H for home wins and an R for road wins, keeping careful columns so she wouldn't be negligent about any game. Darius leaned across her lap, and Kohen kept squinting at her marks like he expected her to cheat. By the time she reached game thirty, a pattern was emerging that surprised all three of them.

"It's not just our team," Kate said slowly. "Look. They won way more than half their home games, but so did the teams they played against, in their own buildings. It's everywhere in the list." She scrolled to a league summary page and found the same thing across the whole sport.

Kohen pointed at a phrase on the screen. "It even has a name. Home advantage."

"So I was right," he said, and then he paused, because Darius was still frowning. "But right in a weird way. It doesn't mean they're bad."

"It means we'd better hope the next game is here," Darius said.

Kate looked at the schedule and laughed. "Game six is at their place." She slid the napkin across the couch so both of them could see her careful columns of letters, and Kohen handed her the last untouched handful of popcorn from the bottom of the bowl.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Keith Johnstone's 1979 book 'Impro' taught that characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama.
story:
Christopher sat on the living room rug with his friend Skye, who had come over to practice for Monday's drama tryout. The criterion for making the improv team was simple: accept every offer with "yes, and," and keep the scene alive. Christopher had practiced alone all week, but alone was easy. With a partner, every time Skye said something, Christopher felt his brain stall, and the scenes kept dying.

"You be the king," Skye said, dropping onto the couch like a throne. "I'll be the servant. Yes, and, your majesty, I've brought your breakfast."

"Yes, and it's cold," Christopher said, trying to sound royal. He straightened his back and looked down his nose. The scene went on for a minute, then flopped. They tried again, and it flopped again. Skye pulled her knees up, watching him with the careful look of someone deciding whether to say what she actually thought.

"Maybe you're doing it wrong on purpose," she said, "to stay safe. You always take the safe part." Christopher started to argue, then stopped, because she was probably right. His dad was circulating through the room with a stack of mail, and Christopher grabbed a package off the pile before it got carried away. Inside was a book his drama teacher had recommended: a 1979 book called "Impro," by Keith Johnstone. Christopher flipped through it while Skye peeled an orange and handed him half without being asked.

"Listen to this," he said. "He says characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama." He read a bit about how a king who bowingly apologizes is suddenly lower status than his servant. Christopher looked at Skye. "So the funny part isn't the king being king. It's the king acting small, or the servant acting big."

They set the scene again. Skye offered the breakfast, and this time Christopher took it and then bowed, groveling, apologizing for the cold toast as if it were his fault. Skye's eyes lit up. "Yes, and I've decided you'll scrub the floors before lunch," she announced, pointing a royal finger. Christopher wailed and thanked her. They were both laughing so hard his dad came back to see what was going on, and Skye gave him the last segment of orange.

On Monday they stood side by side at tryouts, and when the teacher called them up, Christopher wasn't pessimistic anymore, or only a little. The prompt was "lost in a museum." Skye began as a tour guide, grand and booming. Christopher folded himself small, then, line by line, began giving the orders, until he was commanding the guide to follow him. In the third row, someone snorted with laughter.

"Okay, next pair," the teacher said, and underlined something on her clipboard.

"See you at practice Tuesday," Skye whispered.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up.
story:
The end-of-season party was supposed to be fun, but Connor stood at the shallow end of the pool with his slice of pizza going cold and watched his teammates drift apart like leaves on the water. Ephraim was already talking to his mom by the changing rooms. Nathanael sat alone on the diving block, staring at the scoreboard even though the scoreboard was dark. Something felt wrong, and it was not just the chlorine smell or the fact that the pool closed in ninety minutes and they would all be kicked out until next September. The team had been the same all winter, and now it was about to stop being a team, and nobody seemed willing to say so out loud.

Connor sat down next to Nathanael on the block. "You okay?"

"I wanted the record in the fifty free," Nathanael said. "Tonight was my last chance. I missed it by four tenths of a second." He kept his eyes on the empty lanes. "It's weird. Everyone's acting like this is just a normal party."

That was exactly it, Connor thought. Everyone was acting normal, and it was fake, and the fakeness was the weird part. He wondered if there was a name for what happened to a group when it finished its work. While Nathanaim went to look for the record board, Connor drifted toward the coach's office, where Mr. Rahman was stacking kickboards and hauling cones toward the storage closet before the pool manager locked the gates.

"I'm looking for a stopwatch to return," Connor said, which was half true. On the desk lay a fat binder of coaching notes, and one photocopied page had slipped loose. Connor picked it up to put it back and saw a diagram of stages: forming, storming, norming, performing, and then a fifth stage added in 1977 by Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. The word printed beside it was adjourning.

So it was a real thing. Groups that end go through a fifth stage. That meant the strange flat feeling at this party was not just him being dramatic. It had a pattern behind it, something he could not see directly but could test. If the stage existed, then maybe pretending nothing was ending made it worse, and maybe doing something deliberate about the ending would make it better. He had ninety minutes before the doors locked.

He was assertive about it, more than he usually dared to be. He marched back onto the deck and announced one last relay, Sharks versus Sharks, everybody in the water, no excuses. Ephraim laughed, and even Nathanael, who claimed he was done swimming forever, pulled his goggles back on. "This is adjourning," Connor said as they lined up. "The last stage. We do it on purpose instead of just drifting out the door."

They swam. The pool lights made the water radiate a blue glow up into the rafters, and the noise they made echoed like a real meet. Nathanael swam the anchor leg so hard that he touched the wall and just floated there, grinning at the ceiling.

"Same time next season?" Ephraim asked as they toweled off.

Nathanael looked at the dark scoreboard one more time. "Four tenths," he said. "I'll find those four tenths somewhere."

Mr. Rahman stuck his head out of the office. "Pool closes in five minutes, gentlemen."

"Then we go out big," said Connor, and he turned and jumped.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: In belly breathing, also called diaphragmatic breathing, the belly rises as you breathe in instead of the shoulders lifting, which lets the lungs fill more deeply.
story:
Brody sat in the waiting room of the doctor's office with his hands pressed flat against his knees, because if his knees bounced, Jeffrey would notice, and if Jeffrey noticed, Jeffrey would ask, and Brody did not want to explain that his heart had been racing since the hallway outside science class. It had started three weeks ago, around the time his mother began a long commute to her new job, leaving before dark and coming home after dinner. He had told himself it was nothing. But this morning his hands had gone cold during a quiz, and Ms. Ahmed had quietly handed him a pass to the nurse, who had set up this appointment.

"Dude, you look like you're waiting for a burial," Jeffrey whispered. Jeffrey had come along because the nurse needed someone to walk him over, and also because Jeffrey never missed anything.

The nurse called them both back to a small room and said the doctor would be a few minutes. A poster on the wall showed a person lying down with one hand on the stomach. Brody read the small print. Belly breathing, also called diaphragmatic breathing, it said, means the belly rises as you breathe in instead of the shoulders lifting, which lets the lungs fill more deeply.

"That's it?" Brody said. "That's what she's going to teach me?"

"Put your hand on your stomach," Jeffrey said, already doing it himself. "I want to see if I do it right."

Brody laid his palm on his belly and breathed the way he normally did. His shoulders rose. His stomach stayed flat. He tried again, forcing his shoulders down, and this time his belly lifted like a small balloon under his hand. "Oh," he said. "It actually works the other way."

"So we've both been breathing wrong our whole lives," Jeffrey said, grinning.

When Ms. Ahmed had handed him the pass that morning, Brody had felt a hot flicker of resentment, as if she were announcing his weakness to the whole row. Now, in the little room, he wondered whether she had simply noticed what he had spent three weeks hiding from himself. He couldn't decide, and the question sat there, unresolved, while he practiced. In, belly up. Out, belly down. His cold hands warmed. His heart slowed from a drumroll to something steadier.

The doctor came in and talked with him about sleep too, about screens off at nine and a regular bedtime even on Fridays, and Brody wrote it on his arm because he would lose a paper. Walking out through the waiting room, he felt almost buoyant, like a cork pushed down and let go.

"Same time tomorrow?" Jeffrey asked. "Belly check in the cafeteria?"

"Only if you put your hand on your stomach first," Brody said. "So everyone stares at you, not me."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Lowering the coverslip onto the slide at an angle, one edge first, helps push out air so fewer bubbles form over the cells.
story:
Nora pressed her eye to the microscope and saw dozens of round black-edged circles crowding the field, and she sat back with a groan. Across the lab table at the science museum, Renaud leaned over his own scope, smug as anything. "Mine has beautiful cells," he announced. "Brick-shaped. Lined up like a wall." He wanted to win the museum's junior microscopist badge before anyone else in their class, and today was the last day of the workshop.

Mr. McKenzie, who ran the lab, had told them to peel a paper-thin layer of onion skin, lay it on a slide, add one drop of iodine, and cover it. Nora had done all of that. She had even been careful. But her circles were everywhere, and when she tried to label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus on her worksheet, she faced an acute dilemma: she could not find a single cell.

Hawa, working beside her, slid her chair over. "Those aren't cells," she said. "They're air bubbles." Nora frowned at the worksheet. "How do you know?" "Because cells don't have black rims and bubbles do. I got bubbles my first try too, on Tuesday." Hawa's want was quieter than Renaud's; she was saving her good slides for her grandmother, who had been a lab technician and could no longer see well enough to use a microscope herself. She wanted to describe the cells to her perfectly, every part named.

Nora thought back to how she had dropped the coverslip. She had let it fall flat, straight down, like a lid on a jar. Maybe the falling glass trapped air under it. She tried a different way, slow and deliberate: she touched one edge of the coverslip to the drop first, then lowered the rest at an angle, letting it settle edge by edge across the onion skin. One edge first, she told herself, like closing a door gently instead of slamming it.

When she looked again, the field was almost clean. Rows of brick-shaped cells stretched out before her, each with a clear outer wall, a thin line of membrane just inside it, and a dark dot of a nucleus sitting near the center. Renaud came to look, and his smugness provoked Nora into something like triumph. "Fewer bubbles," she said, not even hiding it. "Lowering it at an angle pushes the air out." Renaud grabbed a new coverslip and tilted it carefully over his slide, tongue between his teeth.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The vertical columns of the periodic table are called groups, and elements in the same group tend to have similar chemical properties.
story:
The garage smelled like oil and old cardboard, and Ivy had taped a giant printout of the periodic table to the wall between the bikes. She was supposed to be studying for Mr. Nguyen's quiz, but her dad had already sold the workbench, and half the shelves were empty boxes now, because they were moving at the end of the month. She figured if she couldn't keep the garage, she could at least keep the table.

Rylan sat on an overturned milk crate, spinning a lug nut. "You're staring at it like it's going to talk."

"It kind of does." Ivy traced her finger down the far right edge of the chart. "Helium, neon, argon. They're all stacked in the same column, and Mr. Nguyen kept tapping that column with his marker like it meant something." She'd spent a whole class wondering, and when she finally asked him, he'd just said, "The vertical columns are called groups," and moved on, which had felt like being handed a locked box with the key withheld.

"Groups," Rylan repeated, unimpressed. "So they're... a club?"

"That's what I want to know." She flipped through her notes, looking for the trick Mr. Nguyen had shown them: the big number on each tile, the atomic number, told you the protons. Two for helium, ten for neon, eighteen for argon. She wrote the numbers in chalk on the garage floor, one above another, like footprints. Then she tested her idea. If being in a group meant anything, maybe it should hold for a column she hadn't studied. She picked the left edge, lithium and sodium, and checked their tiles. One difference between their numbers. She checked helium to neon. Another difference, the same one. Down every column she tried, the pattern repeated, tidy as teeth. Her idea was holding up so far it felt almost credible, like the whole table was built on rails she couldn't see.

"That's it," she said. "Elements in the same group act alike. That's the whole secret."

Rylan stopped spinning the lug nut. He'd been insisting all week that chemistry was just memorization, worse than the tendon diagram they'd had to label in biology, because at least tendons were real things you could point to on your own ankle. Now he leaned over the chalk numbers, squinting. "Okay," he said slowly. "Okay, that's not just memorizing. That's like a rule under the rule." He picked up the chalk and drew his own column, copper and silver stacked together, and waited for her to nod.

Outside, a moving truck honked twice on the street, and Ivy thought of last summer, when the three of them, her, Rylan, and Alicia, had turned this same garage into a lab and let a bowl of fruit decompose on the shelf for a "crystal experiment" that never worked. Alicia wasn't coming over anymore; she'd moved in the spring, and now Ivy was the one leaving. She rubbed her sleeve across the chalk until the numbers blurred into gray dust.

She tore the printout off the wall, folded it into quarters, and handed it to Rylan. "You're taking this," she said. "You already started your own column."

He tucked it inside his jacket like it was a map, and drew one more thing in the chalk dust: an arrow, pointing at the empty space she'd left on the floor.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: In tropical rainforests, the difference between day and night temperatures can be larger than the difference between the warmest and coolest months.
story:
The trail climbed out of the pines into an open stretch of rock, and Charles stopped to catch his breath beside Mr. Aquino, who was holding a folder of printed graphs even on a hike. "Rainfall and temperature," Mr. Aquino said, tapping the folder. "Desert versus rainforest. You'll present it next week, so keep thinking while we walk." Charles had the desert graph memorized already, all fierce spikes and long flat stretches of nothing, but the rainforest one kept confusing him, and that was the problem he wanted solved before Monday.

Fateh jogged up beside them, camera bouncing on its strap. His want was simpler and louder: he was trying to photograph a woodpecker for the trail club's end-of-year display, and so far he had three blurry pictures of branches. "It was right there," he said, pointing at a dead snag ahead. "If you two would stop talking, maybe it would come back."

Charles spread the two graphs on a flat boulder while the others ate. The bars for monthly rainfall looked like two different worlds, almost none for the desert, heavy and steady all year for the rainforest. The temperature lines were stranger. The desert line rose and fell with the seasons, but the rainforest line ran nearly level across the whole year. "Warm every month," Charles said slowly, tracing it with his finger. "So why did the trip packing list say to bring a sweater?" His class had a rainforest trip in the spring, and his mother had read the list out loud at dinner, which had made no sense to him at all.

Cristiano leaned over his shoulder, chewing a granola bar. "A sweater for the rainforest? That's a phenomenon I'd like to see." He turned the page, and there it was, a second smaller chart they had all skipped, showing day against night at one rainforest station. The day temperature sat high. The night temperature dropped far below it. Charles laid his ruler along the two lines and measured the gap, then went back and measured the yearly line. The day-to-night gap was bigger. "So the sweater isn't for a cold month," he said. "There isn't a cold month. It's for the nights." The rule he'd been missing had been hiding in the graph he'd ignored.

"I still don't get how it can be hot all year but cold at night," Fateh said, crouching to get a low angle on the snag. Charles started to answer, then stopped. He didn't know why, only that the chart said it did, and that felt like enough to stand on for now. "The graph doesn't say why," he admitted. "It just says how much." Cristiano nodded like that settled it, and Charles wrote "night gap bigger than month gap" in the margin, underlined twice.

They hiked on through the afternoon shade. Charles thought about how his own body had to regulate its temperature when the trail went from sun to shadow, and how the desert graph showed a place that swung with the whole year while the rainforest swung with every single day. Two different rhythms, both readable in lines and bars, if you looked at the right chart.

Near the trailhead, a woodpecker landed on the snag and started hammering. Fateh raised his camera with shaking hands and held his breath. Cristiano grabbed Charles's sleeve and pointed without a word. The shutter clicked three times, quick and quiet, and then the bird swept off over the trees, a flash of black and white against the late light. Fateh looked down at the screen and whispered, "I got it. I actually got it."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in jars; maggots grew in open jars, but not in jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat.
story:
The August air hung humid over the garden, and Luke crouched beside the compost bin where Angel was pointing at a cloud of tiny flies. "See?" Angel said, jabbing a finger at a mushy peach. "The fruit makes them. It rots, and then the flies just appear. My grandpa says the same thing about garbage. It's a known fact." Luke watched one of the flies land on the peach, crawl a few steps, then lift off again, and a question formed in his mind so fast he almost said it out loud. Appear from where, exactly?

"My cousin had a book about a guy named Redi," Luke said slowly, picking up a fallen tomato. "In 1668 he put meat in jars. Maggots grew in the open jars, but not in the ones covered with gauze." He turned the tomato over. The gauze had kept the flies off the meat. So what was keeping the flies off Angel's theory? "Do you want to test it?" Angel crossed his arms. "Test what? I already told you it's a fact." But Angel wanted to win the school science fair more than anything, and Luke could see the idea land. "Fine," Angel said. "But if I'm right, my project writes itself."

They raided the shed for two glass jars and a scrap of window screen from Mr. Robinson's scrap bucket by the fence. In each jar went a slice of overripe pear from the ground under the tree. Luke stretched the screen over one jar and snapped the lid ring over it; the other stayed open. He set them side by side on the flat stone by the roses, where the sun would find them. "My hypothesis," Luke said, "is that flies have to reach the fruit first. If I'm wrong, we'll get flies in both." Angel wrote the words on his hand with a pen, frowning at the spelling.

For three days the jars sat there. On the second morning Mr. Robinson leaned over the fence, watering can in hand, and asked what on earth they were growing. "Flies," Angel said gloomily, "or maybe no flies." The old man laughed and moved on. Luke checked the jars every day after his paper route, and his conscience pinched a little on day two, because part of him hoped Angel was right; a mystery would have been more fun than an answer.

On the fourth day the open jar held a dozen specks crawling on the pear, and tiny flies balanced on the glass. The screened jar held only a pear going brown, and nothing else. Angel stared at it for a long moment. "Okay," he said. "Okay, so the flies come from outside. They land on it and, whatever, then there are more flies." He was already scribbling on his hand again. "Redi. 1668. Gauze. This is going to be a great project."

Luke grinned and picked up the screened jar to carry it to the porch, and as he lifted it, a single fruit fly crawled out from under the rim of the screen, where Angel's thumb had bent it loose when he'd "helped" seal it, and drifted down toward the open jar. "You saw nothing," Angel said, pressing the screen flat.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: In Mexican tradition, a quinceañera, the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually begins with a Mass of thanksgiving.
story:
Jade slipped out of the kitchen and into the garage, where her uncle's van sat loaded with cargo for the party: folded chairs, coolers, boxes of favors tied with ribbon.
