She pressed her back against the van's cold door and took out the index card. "A reading from the letter of Saint Paul," she whispered, and got exactly four words further before the words slid apart like dropped beads.

Inside, the family gathering was loud with clinking dishes and her little cousins thundering past. Tomorrow was the big day, and she was supposed to stand up in front of everyone and deliver the reading without the card. Tomorrow. She mouthed the first line again, and again it fell apart halfway through.

Her friend Coby had come along for the dinner, and he found her there, holding a bag of napkins he'd been sent to fetch. "You're hiding," he said.

"I'm not hiding. I'm memorizing." She held up the card as proof. "It's not working."

Coby squinted at it. "You've been sitting still, haven't you? You memorized the whole cafeteria menu pacing in the lunch line."

That gave her an idea, and ideas were testable. She started walking the length of the garage, one lap per sentence, and by the third lap the rhythm of her steps was carrying the words along with it. It wasn't magic, exactly, but it was something she could measure: one lap, two laps, and the third sentence stuck. She was on lap five when her abuela appeared in the doorway, napkin bag forgotten in Coby's hands.

"Mija, that card." Her abuela took it, read it, and pressed her lips together. "This is the English one. You're reading at the Mass. The quinceañera begins with the Mass of thanksgiving, before any party."

"The Mass first?" Jade said. "Before the hall, before the chairs, before everything?"

"Before everything. That's how it goes."

She had memorized the wrong language all week. The two versions were distinct enough that her laps wouldn't simply transfer, and panic rose until her abuela pulled a folded paper from her apron pocket, worn soft at the creases. "Start here. You have tonight."

So Jade paced the garage under the bare bulb, her abuela correcting a word on lap two and nodding on lap three, while Coby counted laps out loud like a coach. By the time her uncle came to hitch the trailer, she made it through the whole reading once without stopping.

"Again," her abuela said, and settled onto a crate to listen.

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: A pivot table summarises a long list of rows by grouping them, for example turning hundreds of survey responses into one row per grade.
story:
Mathis sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with his laptop open and a stack of printed survey pages beside him, wondering if four hundred and thirty rows of answers could actually make anyone crazy. The student council had asked the whole school which new club they wanted most, and somehow Mathis had volunteered to count the results. Mahee had texted him twice already, asking if the summary was ready, and he had answered both times with an approximate number he'd made up by eyeballing the pages. That felt like cheating.

"Four hundred rows," he said to the empty room. "There has to be a way to make the computer count them."

Each row was one student's answer: their grade and their club choice. He knew the seventh graders wanted a robotics club. Probably. He'd read enough rows to feel it, but feelings weren't going to survive Mrs. Teller's question at Thursday's meeting: "Which grade wants what, exactly?"

He typed a message to Mahee.

"Help. 430 survey rows. If I count them by hand I will be here until graduation. Does your cousin's spreadsheet thing do anything for this?"

The reply came fast. "She said try a pivot table. It groups stuff. Like all the answers for a grade turn into one row."

Mathis stared at the words. One row per grade. The whole long list, folded up into something he could actually look at? He found the button, dragged the grade column into one box and the club column into another, and held his breath. The screen rebuilt itself. Where four hundred and thirty rows had been, there were now four. One per grade, each with counts.

He leaned closer. Sixth grade: art club, one hundred and twelve votes. Seventh grade: robotics, ninety-eight. Eighth grade, though, was the surprise. Drama club had one hundred and four votes, not robotics, which was what he'd assumed all week because his friends wouldn't stop talking about it. His friends had hidden the answer from him without knowing it.

He tested it, because he didn't fully trust a machine that worked that fast. He picked ten random rows from the printed pages and counted them by hand, then checked them against the pivot table's numbers. All ten matched. He tried flipping the rows and columns the other way, and suddenly he could see it by club instead of by grade. Two different windows onto the same four hundred and thirty answers.

"Mahee, it worked," he typed. "Eighth grade wants drama. I was wrong all week. This thing is magic."

"It's not magic, it's math," she wrote back. "Bring snacks to the meeting."

Then a new message appeared, from Kaelyn, the council president. "My mom says the principal has to authorize any new club before we announce results. Can you send your summary tonight so she can look at it first?"

Mathis copied the pivot table, pasted it into an email, and looked at the four tidy rows on the screen. Somewhere in his head, the stack of paper on the carpet had already stopped being scary.

"Coming right up," he typed, and hit send.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The word algebra comes from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
story:
Charlie stared at the whiteboard where Mr. Thompson had written x + 7 = 12, and her stomach dropped. Everyone else in the room seemed to know what to do, pencils scratching, while she sat there with a blank page.

"You do the same thing to both sides," Hunter whispered across the aisle. "Like a scale. Take seven off one side, take seven off the other."

"Who told you that?" Charlie whispered back.

"My brother. He failed pre-algebra twice, so he's kind of an expert now."

Charlie tried it. If she took seven from the left side, the x stood alone. If she took seven from the right, twelve became five. So x had to be five. She checked it by putting five back into the original problem: five plus seven really was twelve. It worked, and something in her chest loosened. It was like a hidden rule underneath the numbers, invisible until you tested it.

After class, Mr. Thompson stopped her at the door. "Charlie, hold on. You're my candidate for the regional math team. It's a prestigious program, only two students per school. There's a short presentation requirement, though. You'd need a topic by Friday."

That night she sat at the kitchen table while her mom consumed an entire bowl of popcorn over her own paperwork, and Charlie hunted through library books for a topic. Then she found it, in a chapter about where math words came from. She read the page three times, then grabbed her phone and called Hunter.

"Listen to this," she said. "The word algebra. It comes from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi."

"Wait, so algebra was a book title first?"

"Part of one. Al-jabr. It started as that." She could hardly sit still. She had a topic, and it made the whole subject feel different, like the x on the board had a history.

On Friday she stood in front of Mr. Thompson's desk and gave her two-minute presentation. When she finished, he leaned back.

"Good. One question. If al-Khwarizmi could solve equations without our notation, what do you think he'd make of your scale trick?"

Charlie paused. Then she smiled slowly. "I think he'd say check it. Do the same thing to both sides and see if it still balances."

"Then show me," Mr. Thompson said, and slid a fresh problem across the desk: 3x - 4 = 11.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: A chapati cooks on a hot, dry griddle in only a minute or two, which is why flatbreads are usually made last.
story:
The kitchen smelled like onions and ambition, and Lea was grinning at three recipes taped to the fridge like mission briefings. "Tonight," she announced to the empty room, "rice, curry, and chapatis, all ready at the same time." Her parents were due home at seven, and she wanted the whole meal steaming on the table when they walked in, like she had conjured it. She had talked to Mercedes about it at school, and Mercedes had been so excited she'd demanded a full report by tomorrow, maybe even leftovers.

Lea attacked the chapatis first, because they seemed like the hardest part. She mixed flour and water, rolled thin circles, and laid them one by one on the hot, dry griddle. Each one puffed slightly and was done in barely a minute or two, which startled her, but she pushed on through the stack until all twelve sat in a cloth-covered basket. Then she started the curry. The onions browned, the spices hissed, the tomatoes broke down, and somewhere in there she realized the rice was still uncooked. By the time everything else landed on the table, an hour and a half later, the chapatis had gone cold and stiff as cafeteria trays. She texted Mercedes a photo with the caption "help."

Mercedes called her within minutes. "That happened to my aunt once," Mercedes said. "She said a chapati only needs a minute or two on a hot, dry griddle, so that's why flatbreads are made last. You made them first, didn't you?"

"Yes," Lea groaned, "like a rookie."

"So do them last, obviously." Mercedes paused. "Also, do NOT put oil near the open flame, my aunt called the curry pot extremely flammable and I'm trusting you with that information."

Friday gave her a second chance. Mr. Aziz, her neighbour from two doors down, had heard about her plan through her dad and had dropped off a bag of his preferred atta flour with a note reading "for the bread, when the curry is nearly done." Lea reread the note three times, because the timing was the whole secret hiding inside it. The chapatis took almost no time at all, so they had to come last, folded into the final minutes like the encore of a show. She wrote a timeline on the whiteboard, calculated the median cooking time of everything, and put the rice on first because it took the longest, then the curry, and penciled "CHAPATIS, LAST" in enormous capitals.

At six forty, the curry was bubbling, the rice resting with its lid on, and Lea's hands were dusted white as she rolled the final circle. The griddle hissed. She watched the bread puff in under two minutes, flipped it, and slid it into a warmed towel just as headlights swept the driveway. Her parents came through the door into a wall of steam and spice, and her dad actually stopped in his tracks. "You made all this?" Lea was already rolling the last ball of dough. "Made it," she said, "and timed it. Grab a plate."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Some linear equations have no solution, such as x + 1 = x + 2, because no number is one more and two more than itself at once.
story:
Nolan spread his homework across the kitchen table and pulled the last worksheet toward him, the one Mr. Silva had marked with a star. "Star problems count double," Mr. Silva had said, and Nolan needed the points, because his quiz average was sitting at a 68.

The first ones went fine. For x + 5 = 12, he subtracted 5 from both sides and got x = 7, which checked out when he plugged it back in. For 2x - 3 = 9, he added 3 to both sides, then divided both sides by 2, and x = 6 fell out neatly. He was starting to feel like he actually understood the rule: whatever you do to one side, you do to the other, like a scale that has to stay balanced.

Then he hit the star problem: x + 1 = x + 2. He subtracted x from both sides and got 1 = 2. He stared at that. He tried again, subtracting 1 from both sides instead, and got x = x + 1. He subtracted x again and landed back at 0 = 1. His pencil left a grey smear where he had erased so many times.

His friend Everley texted back when he sent a photo of the problem. "did you try dividing?" He wrote back that he had, and that he'd tried multiplying too, and every time the x's just cancelled out and left him with numbers that contradicted each other. He kept testing his idea that he was making an arithmetic slip somewhere, checking each step like a detective, but every path ended the same way.

Then he stopped with his pencil in the air. He wasn't slipshod at arithmetic; the problem itself was the trick. No number could be one more than itself and two more than itself at the same time. That was impossible for any number he could name. He tested it with x = 10: 11 on the left, 12 on the right. With x = 100: 101 and 102. Always one apart. There wasn't some hidden number that would work, the way there had been for the easier problems. He wrote at the bottom of the problem, "No solution," and it felt strange to write that, like admitting defeat, except it wasn't one.

His mother slid a plate of toast across the table. "Stuck?" she asked. "The opposite," Nolan said, and circled his answer twice. "Mr. Silva said some of these would try to fool us. I think this one's the fooler." He took a bite of toast and flipped to the next problem, 3x + 2 = 3x + 2, where every number he tried worked. He grinned and wrote, "All numbers," then paused, pencil hovering. "Or is that one trivial?"

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, time goes along the horizontal axis and distance goes up the vertical axis.
story:
Tyler set his notebook on the kitchen table, and his father held the stopwatch. On Monday, science class had rolled a ball down a ramp and Mr. Santos-Reyes had assigned each student the same job: measure how far the ball rolled across the floor at each second, then turn those numbers into a distance-time graph. The problem was that Tyler's measurements had come out wrong twice, and the assignment was due tomorrow.

"Okay," he said. "On three."

His father clicked the stopwatch, and Tyler's little brother's soccer ball rolled off the table edge, bounced once, and traveled across the kitchen tile. At one second it passed the first pencil Tyler had laid down as a marker. At two seconds it passed the second. It slowed, wobbled, and stopped just past the fourth pencil.

"Two point four meters, four seconds," his father read off.

"Third time in a row," Tyler said. "Good. Now I can replicate the whole thing upstairs in the hallway, since the graph needs more than one trial." He wrote the numbers down and frowned at them. Something still wasn't right, and he couldn't see what. The ball always went about the same distance each second, slowing near the end, and he had plenty of data. He climbed the stairs, laid out the pencils again, and ran three more trials while Leighton timed them on his phone over video chat.

Then he drew the graph. He put distance along the bottom of the page and time going up the side, because that was how he'd imagined it, like filling a container. The line came out nearly straight and steep at the start, then shot almost sideways, and it made no sense at all. It looked like the ball had traveled an enormous amount of time in almost no distance.

"That can't be right," Leighton said through the phone speaker. "Mine looks completely different."

Tyler leaned over his own graph on Leighton's screen. Leighton's line curved gently upward, small at first, then steeper. It was ironic, Tyler thought, that he'd spent all evening getting perfect measurements and then ruined them with one stroke of a pencil. He flipped through his notes until he found the sentence he'd copied from the board: time goes along the horizontal axis and distance goes up the vertical axis. He had written it down and then drawn everything backward.

He tore out the page and started again, time marching across the bottom, distance climbing the side. The new line rose slowly and then leveled off where the ball had lost its momentum.

"There," he said, holding it up to the camera. "Now it tells the story of the ball."

"Draw me one more," Leighton said. "I want to see if my hallway matches yours."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: Hindus usually cremate the dead, returning the body to the five elements, though young children and some holy people are traditionally buried instead.
story:
Evan spread his notebook across the kitchen table and drew a line down the middle of the page. On the left he wrote CHRISTIAN and on the right he wrote HINDU. The assignment from Mr. Morin was to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death, and it was due Friday. The whole thing intimidated him, because he had been to exactly one funeral in his life, his grandmother's, and he had mostly remembered the sandwiches afterward.

He wrote "heaven" on the left side. That part he knew from Sunday school and from things his mom said at the funeral, about grandmother being in a better place. The right side stayed blank until he remembered that his classmate Dhruv was Hindu. Evan called him.

"Do you guys believe in heaven?" he asked when Dhruv picked up.

"Sort of, but not like yours," Dhruv said. "We get reborn. The soul comes back in a new body, over and over, until it finally stops being reborn." Evan wrote "rebirth" and "soul comes back" on the right side of his line. He asked about funerals, since his grandmother's had been at a church with a casket.

"We cremate," Dhruv said. "Burn the body, return it to the five elements. Earth, water, fire, air, sky."

"Everybody?" Evan asked. He had a theory now: if the soul leaves and gets reborn, then cremation must be the rule for everyone, no exceptions. It fit together neatly, like a math proof.

"No, actually," Dhruv said, and Evan's theory fell apart on the spot. "Babies and really young kids, and some holy people, get buried instead."

"Wait, buried? Like us?"

"Like you guys, yeah. My little cousin, she was only four months old when she died. She was buried."

Evan sat with the phone against his shoulder. There was a certain irony in the fact that the two faiths, which his chart made look like opposites, buried some of their dead in exactly the same way. He wrote "babies and holy people buried" on the right side and drew an arrow across the middle of the page to the left side, where he added "buried too."

On Thursday he showed the chart to Mr. Morin, who read it and then looked up. "Good, you kept it factual," he said. "Religion can be a controversial subject, so some students shy away from the details. You didn't." He handed it back and moved on to Veer's table, where Veer was arguing that ghosts should count as an afterlife.

At home that evening, Evan added one more line at the bottom of the page in his smallest printing: Ask Dhruv about the five elements again, which one is sky? He underlined it twice and closed the notebook.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Tempo is measured in beats per minute, so a marking of 60 means one beat each second.
story:
The metronome app on Willow's phone had crashed twice, so Mr. Romano's studio wall clock was doing the job instead. She watched the second hand sweep while her left hand practiced the opening of the nocturne, one chord per tick. Mr. Romano had pencilled a number over the first measure: 60.

"Sixty," said Jolene, who was sprawled on the bench beside her, waiting for her own lesson. "Is that like a grade?"

"It's tempo. Tempo is measured in beats per minute, so sixty means one beat each second." Willow tapped the page. "That's why he sent me to the clock. The app was lying to me anyway. It kept telling me sixty when it felt like ninety."

She counted her chords against the second hand. The first few lined up. Then she drifted, one chord ahead of the tick, then two. She stopped and stared at the clock as if it had insulted her. The problem wasn't her fingers, which were resilient enough after four years of scales. The problem was that she was speeding up without noticing, and she couldn't hear it happening. Slow creeping changes were invisible that way. Fast ones, like the sudden loud part in measure seventeen, she could catch, because the dynamics there were obvious, a jump from quiet to slamming. The drift was quieter than the music.

So she tested it. She installed the free metronome app again on Jolene's phone instead, since Jolene's phone had better hygiene and no cracked screen, and propped it on the music rack with the sound off, using only the flashing light. She played the opening with her eyes flicking between the light and the clock's second hand. Whenever the two disagreed, she knew the phone was off, not her. The clock, at least, never lied.

Three ticks behind. That was her drift, over the first eight bars. Not huge, but enough that by the middle section, where the tempo marking changed, she'd be a full beat ahead of any accompanist. Mr. Romano came back in with his coffee and watched the flashing light with mild suspicion.

"New metronome?" he said.

"New experiment," Willow said, and started the piece again from the top, eyes on the light, second hand turning away in the corner of her vision.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Delayed muscle soreness is not caused by lactic acid, which returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise.
story:
Hunter's second practice of the season ended with twenty laps around the outfield, and the next morning his legs felt like someone had filled them with wet sand. He limped onto the school bus and dropped into the seat beside Nathalie, who was reading a novel with her knees drawn up against the seatback in front of her.

"Rough day?" she asked.

"Rough day after a day," Hunter said. "Practice was yesterday. I was fine at dinner, fine this morning when I woke up, and then around second period my thighs started screaming. Explain that."

At the diamond that afternoon, Tyler had an answer ready. "Lactic acid," he announced, swinging his bat like a veteran showing off his stance. "It builds up when you run, and it makes you sore. My cousin told me. You've got to stretch it out before it hardens."

Hunter thought about that while he orbited the bases during warm-ups, jogging the loop from first to home. Tyler's explanation did not fit what had happened to him. His legs had felt fine right after practice, fine an hour later, fine at bedtime. The soreness had shown up the next day, like a bill arriving late. Whatever had caused it, it was something that worked slowly, not something left over from the running itself. He decided to test it. If leftover acid from yesterday was the problem, then warming up slowly and sweating it out should help, and the soreness should ease as practice went on. If something else was going on, the soreness would behave differently.

He jogged, he stretched, he took his turns in the field. His legs stayed sore, and by the last inning they were worse, but in an ordinary tired way, not in a way that felt like something draining out of him. After practice he sat on the bench with his phone and typed out a message to Nathalie: "You know anything about lactic acid? Tyler says it's why I'm sore, but I wasn't sore until a day after practice. That doesn't add up."

Her reply came while he was unlacing his cleats. "Look it up. Mr. Kaminski has that sports science book in his room, the blue one on the shelf by the window."

Mr. Kaminski was still locking the equipment shed, so Hunter caught him at the gate. "Can I borrow the blue book tomorrow?" he asked. "The one about muscles."

"Take it tonight if you want," Mr. Kaminski said, and handed over the key ring so Hunter could walk back with him and pull it off the shelf himself.

At the kitchen table, Hunter turned to the chapter on recovery and ran his finger down the page. There it was, in plain print: soreness that starts a day or more after hard exercise is not caused by lactic acid. Lactic acid returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise. Hunter read the sentence twice, then pulled out his phone.

"Tyler," he typed, "your acid would've been gone before I even got home. Normal in about an hour after exercise. You owe me a soda." He hit send and went back to the chapter while the storm of Tyler's turbulent reply buzzed in, unread, against the table.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Robert Hooke named cells in his 1665 book Micrographia after seeing tiny compartments in a thin slice of cork under his microscope.
story:
The waiting room of the vet clinic smelled like dog shampoo and coffee, and George had memorized both smells by now, because every Tuesday he waited there until his mom finished her shift in the back. Tonight, though, Mr. Gagnon had waved him into the lab. "We keep the old microscope back here," the vet had said. "Science homework?"

"Onion cells," George said. "I have to draw them and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus, and my teacher wants it by tomorrow." At home his little cousin had knocked his own microscope off the shelf, and the school's had a lens so foggy it made every cell look like a ghost.

He peeled a paper-thin layer of onion skin from a slice in his lunch bag, laid it on a slide, and lowered the lens. His breath condensed on the cold glass until he remembered to breathe through his mouth. Then the image snapped into focus, and there they were: row after row of little boxes, each one outlined, each one with a dark dot near its middle. He grabbed his pencil.

Caelan, who had come along to pick up his cat's medicine, leaned over George's shoulder. "Okay, that's weird. They look exactly like the drawing at the science museum. The cork one."

"What cork one?"

"That giant old book they had open in a case. Robert Hooke, 1665, Micrographia. He drew this thin slice of cork and it had all these tiny boxes, and he called them cells." Caelan tapped the slide. "Same word that's on your worksheet."

George sat back. So the word he'd copied off the board a hundred times, cell, had come from a man staring at cork three hundred and fifty years before George stared at an onion. "Cells," he said slowly. "Because they looked like little rooms."

"Little prison cells," Caelan said. "Yours are jail cells for onions."

"Ha." George drew the outlines first, then the dots. The nucleus was easy; the wall was the outside line; but the membrane was right against it, thin as a rumor. He tested an idea: if he focused up and down, one layer should sit just inside the other, like a counterfeit dollar printed slightly off from the real one. He turned the fine focus a hair, and there it was, a second boundary hugging the wall.

"Diagnosis," Annabelle announced from the doorway, cat carrier in hand. "Mr. Whiskers has a hairball, and you have a finished worksheet."

"One label left," George said, and printed MEMBRANE along the inner line, right beside Caelan's smudged fingerprint.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah, making the trip west far faster than by wagon.
story:
Mason had picked the thinnest book in the whole stack, a settler's diary from 1866, because he figured thin meant fast. He was wrong. Miriam Caldwell wrote about everything: the oxen, the rivers, her sister's boots. Mason had been at the library table for twenty minutes and had learned only that wagon wheels could erode a person's patience, which was not something he could put in his essay.

Leane dropped into the chair across from him with a stack of her own books and a plan. "I need a topic nobody else will pick," she said. "Everyone's doing the railroad. The railroad is the movie everyone has already seen."

"The railroad's not that interesting," Mason said, mostly because he had no topic at all.

"That's because you don't know the ending. The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on the tenth of May, 1869, at Promontory Summit, Utah." She said it like a weather report. "After that, the trip west was far faster than by wagon. Days instead of months."

Mason looked down at the diary. Miriam Caldwell had crossed the country by wagon, and she had written "month four" on the page he was reading. Month four. He flipped forward, looking for the entry where she arrived. There it was: month six. Six months of mud and a dead ox named Benjamin.

He grabbed a pencil and did the arithmetic on the back of his hand, which Mr. Lau, shelving books two aisles over, would certainly disapprove of if he saw it. If the train could do it in days, then after May of 1869, nobody like Miriam had to eat dust for half a year. So why did thousands of families still go before that? He read the diary again with new eyes, and there it was, scattered through Miriam's complaints. Cheap land. Her father had lost his shop back east when prices went wild; she'd written "a loaf of bread costs what a hat used to," which sounded like inflation, though she never used the word. The land out west was the whole reason, and the railroad was just the faster door to it.

"Leane," he said. "You just gave me my essay."

"Then you owe me a topic nobody has seen."

"Try the buffalo. They nearly went endangered after all this, everybody hunting from the trains." He wasn't sure that was in his textbook, but it felt true, and Leane was already writing it down.

Mr. Lau passed the table on his way to the cart. "Six months by wagon," Mason told him, pointing at the diary. "Days by train, after 1869."

Mr. Lau looked at the pencil marks on the back of Mason's hand and held out a pad of sticky notes without a word.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: Freytag's pyramid, based on Gustav Freytag's 1863 book on drama, pictures a plot as rising to the climax at its peak and then falling.
story:
Lily sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her notebook open to page three, which was really page seven, because pages four through six were crossed out so hard the ink had saturated the paper and bled through to the other side. Her short story was due tomorrow, and Mr. Almeida had written one thing at the top of her draft: "Where is the climax?" She had a girl, a flooded creek, and a stranded dog, but nothing rose or fell. The story just lay there, flat as spilled water.

Her phone buzzed. It was Frederick, calling from his kitchen three houses down. "Is your story done?" he asked. "Because mine is six sentences long and I'm calling it finished."

"Mine has a problem," Lily said. "Mr. Almeida says nothing builds. Everything happens in one paragraph and then it stops."

"Sounds like my last geography grade," Frederick said. There was a pause, and then the sound of him chewing something. "Wait, my sister has this poster. Hold on." Lily heard a door, a thump, and a muffled argument with someone unnamed. He came back out of breath. "Okay, it's called Freytag's pyramid. Gustav Freytag, 1863, a book on drama. It pictures a plot as rising to the climax at its peak and then falling."

Lily grabbed the back of her mythology worksheet and flipped it over. "Say that again, slower."

"Rising to the climax at the peak," Frederick repeated, "and then falling. Like a mountain. My sister says it's why every movie feels the same."

She hung up on him without saying goodbye, which she would apologize for later, and drew a mountain. At the bottom she wrote "girl hears dog." Halfway up the slope she wrote "creek rises." Then, at the peak, she wrote nothing, because that was the whole problem. She stared at the empty summit and understood something she hadn't been able to see on the lined pages: she had been saving the dog in paragraph two, when the dog needed to be saved at the top.

She rewrote the ending twice. The second time, she gave the girl and the dog's owner an actual argument on the bank of the creek, and she had to stop and fix the quotation marks three times because the comma kept landing on the wrong side. "Get in the boat," the girl said, "before the water takes the whole dock." She read it aloud to the wall and the wall did not laugh at her, which felt like progress after the humiliation of reading aloud in class on Tuesday, when her voice had cracked on the word "creek" and Devin had repeated it in a squeak until the teacher shut him down and half the room still giggled, laughter being contagious in exactly the way the flu is.

Her mother called up that dinner was ready, and Lily yelled down one minute, and then wrote for eleven more minutes, because the falling side of the mountain needed its own paragraph, and falling turned out to be harder than climbing. Things had to get quieter, not just end.

At dinner she pushed noodles around her plate and thought about the ending. Her mother asked if something was wrong at school. "No," Lily said. "Something's almost right." That was true and not true. The story was done, printed, in her bag by the door. But at the last second she had written a final line she hadn't planned, one where the dog's owner looks back across the water and sees someone else standing on the far bank, and she didn't know who it was, and she hadn't fixed it, and tomorrow Mr. Almeida was going to ask her.

She carried her plate to the sink and then went back up and read the line one more time. "Someone was standing on the far bank," she said to the empty room. "Someone was."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
Beatrice taped the last page of her chart to the gym wall and stepped back to look at it. The column headers read Player, Points, Games Played, and then a blank column she had labeled Average. For two weeks she had sat in the bleachers with a notebook, tracking every basket in lunchtime pickup games, because Ms. Sharma had announced that only the top three scorers would participate in the exhibition game against the neighbouring school.

"You're fourth," Amine said, walking over with a juice box. "Rhea has you beat by like six points."

"That's what the chart on the door says." Beatrice tapped her own paper. "But the door chart only shows total points. Marcus played eleven games. I played six."

Rhea jogged over from the court, still bouncing a ball. "Six? Why so few?"

"My mom had these Saturday shifts, so I missed half the sessions." Beatrice filled in her blank column with quick strokes of her pencil. "If I count points per game instead of points total, look." She held up the page. Rhea leaned in, squinting.

"That says you're first," Rhea said slowly.

Beatrice had gotten the idea from her uncle, at the sports bar in March, when the tournament was on every screen. The Oakland Athletics had come up, and her uncle had leaned across the table and said, "The 2003 book Moneyball by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." Beatrice had asked what undervalued meant, and he had said it meant cheap players everybody overlooked, because the rich teams bought the famous ones. A low-budget team used the numbers to compete with teams that had piles of money. She had thought about that all the way home, about how one number could hide a whole story, and how the famous number everyone stared at was not always the true one.

She took the chart to Ms. Sharma's classroom after last period. The room smelled like whiteboard marker and someone's microwaved lunch gone slightly toxic in the far corner. Ms. Sharma listened while Beatrice pointed at her averages, then at the door chart, then at her averages again.

"You made me a second chart," Ms. Sharma said. "For a game I picked players on."

"You picked on totals. The dodo went to extinction because it couldn't change fast enough, right? I mean, rankings can go extinct too. If the rule changes." Beatrice knew the comparison was weird, but Ms. Sharma smiled anyway.

"Rules matter," Ms. Sharma said. "Who made the rule that we count totals?"

"The announcement just said top three scorers. It never said how." Beatrice set the paper on the desk between them.

Ms. Sharma read the whole chart, top to bottom, tapping each row with her pen. Then she looked out the window toward the gym for a long moment, the way she did before changing a seating plan or cancelling a quiz. "The exhibition is Friday," she said finally. "I'll post the new chart. But you should tell Rhea yourself, before she sees it on the door."

That was the part Beatrice had not planned. She found Rhea at her locker the next morning and turned her phone around to show the photo of the averages, and Rhea stared at it in silence long enough that the hallway noise seemed to get louder around them.

"So I'm second," Rhea said. "You dropped me to second."

"Marcus dropped to third," Amine offered from behind them, unhelpfully.

Rhea closed her locker. "Fine. But you're guarding me on Friday, all game, and if you score on me I get to say the chart was rigged."

"Deal," Beatrice said.

Friday afternoon, with two minutes left and the score tied, Rhea stole the ball at half court, drove past Beatrice, and laid it in off the glass. She turned around and grinned. "Told you it was rigged."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Onion skin cells are nearly colourless, so a drop of iodine stain is often added to make the nucleus and cell wall easier to see.
story:
Quinn had the microscope set up on the picnic table, a slice of onion skin trembling on the slide beneath it, and so far she could see almost nothing at all. Ms. Pritchard, who kept chickens and had let Quinn borrow the microscope from her garage, had said the assignment was simple: look, then label the cell wall, the membrane and the nucleus. Quinn had expected to sit down and see them right away, the way you see a diagram in a textbook.

"There's like a ghost of something," Cruz said, squinting into the eyepiece. "Or maybe my eye is making it up."

"Move over." Makena leaned in and adjusted the fine focus with one careful finger. "I see pale boxes. Sort of. Walls, maybe. But the nucleus? Nothing. And the membrane is not happening."

Quinn frowned at the slide. She tried to hypothesize what was wrong: maybe the slice was too thick, or the light was angled badly, or the whole onion was a dud. She peeled an even thinner layer from the onion and started again. Still pale, still nearly invisible, as if the cells had no interest in being watched.

"Maybe we should just draw the boxes and guess where the nucleus goes," Cruz said.

"No." Then Quinn stopped, because the word had come out more rebellious than she meant it to, and Cruz actually took a half step back from the table. Last year, in Ms. Pritchard's kitchen, Quinn had refused to taste the neighbour's honey because she had decided she hated honey without ever trying it, and Ms. Pritchard had just laughed and said, "That's a bias against my bees, then." Quinn had tasted it, and it had been good, and she had changed her mind right there at the counter. She thought of that now. "Sorry," she said. "But guessing is the same thing. We'd just have a bias toward what the diagram in the book looks like instead of what's actually on the slide."

Makena was already digging through the kit Ms. Pritchard had packed, lifting out tweezers, a spare lens, a small brown bottle. "There's iodine in here. Ms. Pritchard stuck it in the side pocket."

Quinn took the dropper, and because onion skin cells are nearly colourless, and a drop of iodine stain is often added to make the nucleus and cell wall easier to see, she let one drop fall onto the edge of the coverslip and watched it spread underneath. She set the slide on the stage and bent to the eyepiece.

The cells bloomed into view like a fence lit by a low sun, every wall a sharp amber line, and in each box a dark round nucleus sat plain as a pebble.

"There it is," Quinn whispered. "Cruz, come look."

He leaned in, then pulled Makena's sleeve. "Draw fast," he said, "before we forget which dot is the membrane and which one is the nucleus."
